summary: Andy Tadman, partner at Theory Ventures (San Francisco, early-stage data/ML investors), shares research on AI automation in the workplace. LLMs are trained to model data distributions, yielding three properties important for automation: transformation (converting formats like PDF to spreadsheet or email to JSON), synthesis (distilling large amounts of information, answering questions), and reasoning (approximating human decision-making, though limited by what humans write down—domain-specific reasoning requires bespoke data collection, which is a differentiating advantage for new companies). When researching automation, Theory breaks workflows to task and subtask levels. A job isn't just core tasks—it includes interpersonal work like meetings. Jobs exist on a volume-complexity spectrum. Complex low-volume jobs (strategic planning) will use co-pilots with humans remaining in the driver seat. Middle-range jobs (customer support) see substantial workflow automation with 40-70% of day-to-day work automatable, with humans as reviewers or escalation paths. High-volume low-complexity jobs (security alerts, CRM prospect lists, supply chain emails) face total disruption because LLMs are already superhuman—competing against rules-based systems, not humans. An LLM 80-90% as reliable as a human can be 10x better because scale doesn't degrade performance. Two portfolio examples illustrate this. Drop Zone AI handles security operations where human analysts only review ~1% of alerts; agentic systems provide 24/7 coverage and cross-customer threat learning. Amp handles customer engagement where rules-based journeys can't handle combinatorial personalization across millions of users; agentic automation discovers new cohorts and shows uplift in satisfaction and retention. Organizations will shrink and invert their pyramids into diamonds, raising challenges such as how to hire and train new employees when entry-level roles disappear. Tadman recaps three principles: break jobs to fundamental tasks, understand the complexity-volume spectrum, and recognize that surrounding context determines organizational impact—relevant for both founders selling to organizations and executives planning transformation. He closes with a note that technology-problem fit is only one factor; pain severity, incentive alignment, market size and structure also determine whether an idea is worth building a business around.

sections.title: Introduction and Theory Ventures Context
sections.summary: Andy Tadman introduces Theory Ventures, a San Francisco early-stage investor in data and ML companies. The talk focuses on where LLMs are most disruptive across job categories, based on research from hundreds of buyers and builders.

sections.title: Three Key LLM Properties for Automation
sections.summary: LLMs model data distributions, producing three properties: transformation (converting between formats), synthesis (distilling information), and reasoning (approximating human decision-making). Domain-specific reasoning requires bespoke data collection, a startup differentiator.

sections.title: Job Decomposition and Workflow Analysis
sections.summary: Theory breaks workflows to task and subtask levels for analysis. A job includes both core tasks and interpersonal work like meetings. Security analyst workflow is used as an example of iterative alert, query, transform, analyze cycles.

sections.title: Volume-Complexity Spectrum and Three Automation Categories
sections.summary: Jobs exist on a volume-complexity spectrum. Complex low-volume jobs get co-pilots; middle-range jobs get core workflow automation (40-70% automatable) with humans as reviewers; high-volume low-complexity jobs face total disruption.

sections.title: Why High-Volume Low-Complexity Jobs Face Total Disruption
sections.summary: High-volume jobs are hard because of scale—teams get overwhelmed and build rules-based automations. Competition becomes AI versus rules-based software, not AI versus human. LLMs can be 10x better because performance doesn't degrade with volume.

sections.title: Drop Zone AI: Security Operations Example
sections.summary: Drop Zone AI builds agentic systems for security operations. Analysts only review 1% of alerts; 4 million global shortage; 12-18 month retention. Agentic systems provide 24/7 coverage, expert query knowledge, perfect memory, and cross-customer threat learning—only needing to beat rules-based systems.

sections.title: Amp: Customer Engagement Example
sections.summary: Amp handles customer engagement where rules-based journeys can't personalize across millions of users. Agentic automation explores messaging variants per user, discovers new cohorts (late-night snackers for a food delivery company), and evaluates long-term impact. Shows uplift in satisfaction and retention through true 1:1 personalization.

sections.title: Organizational Impact and Team Transformation
sections.summary: As LLMs automate high-volume work, organizations will shrink and invert their pyramids into diamonds. Junior IC task-completion roles diminish; remaining positions become managerial or advanced. This raises challenges such as how to hire and train new employees when entry-level roles no longer exist.

sections.title: Recap and Founder Note
sections.summary: Tadman recaps three principles: break jobs to fundamental tasks, understand the complexity-volume spectrum, and recognize surrounding context determines organizational impact. For founders, he notes technology-problem fit is only one factor—pain severity, incentive alignment, market size and structure also determine whether an idea is worth building a business around.

demonstrations: Drop Zone AI: agentic security operations performing end-to-end investigations like a human analyst, providing 24/7 coverage and sharing threat learnings across customers
Amp: agentic customer engagement automation that personalizes messaging per user at scale, discovers new cohorts like late-night snackers, and evaluates impact on long-term retention metrics
